settings.standfirst: You do not need a shelf full of products to make washing less complicated. Start with the water, the cleanser and what happens after the towel.
settings.caption: A quieter routine starts before you turn on the tap.

settings.text:
A shower can be an ordinary part of the day again, rather than another experiment. Before changing every bottle in the bathroom, notice the basics: how warm the water feels, how long you stay under it and whether you rub your skin dry.

The American Academy of Dermatology recommends warm water and a short bath or shower, around 5–10 minutes. Hotter and longer is not the aim. Keep the towel and your usual moisturiser within reach before you start. Read the AAD’s home-care advice.

Less to decide.
More room to listen to your skin.

settings.heading: Choose the cleanser, not the scent

settings.text:
Read the ingredient list, even when the front of a bottle sounds reassuring. The AAD recommends fragrance-free products; “unscented” can still contain ingredients used to mask a smell. A pleasant scent does not tell you how your skin will respond.

The NHS advises using an emollient soap substitute for dry, itchy skin. These wash products do not need a big foam to clean. If you have diagnosed eczema, ask your pharmacist or clinician which wash fits your existing care plan. Read the NHS guide to emollients.

settings.heading: After the shower, keep it gentle

settings.text:
Rinse and pat your skin dry rather than rubbing it. The NHS recommends applying an emollient soon after washing. The AAD also advises moisturising while skin is still damp, and notes that creams or ointments can be more helpful than lighter lotions for eczema-prone skin.

Use the moisturiser that works for you and follow your clinician’s instructions for prescribed treatments. A new body-care routine should sit alongside that plan, not replace it. More on moisturising from the AAD.

settings.heading: Make one change at a time

settings.text: It is easier to understand a routine when you know what changed. Keep a simple note of what you used and how your skin felt, rather than judging everything from one shower.

settings.items:
Keep the water warm and the wash short.
Check the complete ingredient list, including any known allergens.
Have a soft towel and your usual moisturiser ready.
Ask for guidance before replacing prescribed care.

settings.text: The AAD recommends testing new skin-care products before wider use, because ingredients other than fragrance may also irritate. Follow its testing guidance or the plan your clinician gives you. See the AAD’s advice on trying products.

Get medical advice if eczema is not improving with your care plan. The NHS advises urgent assessment if skin suddenly worsens, becomes painful, warm or swollen, leaks fluid or develops pus, or if you have a fever or feel unwell. These can be signs of infection. Read the NHS advice on atopic eczema.
